description: Internal and external growth, public limited companies and how they raise finance.
content_html:
Why Do Businesses Want to Grow?

Once a business has survived its early years, the owners often set their sights on growth. A larger business can spread its fixed costs across more units, negotiate better prices with suppliers and gain a stronger foothold in its market. Growth can happen in two broad ways: internal (organic) growth or external (inorganic) growth. Choosing the right method depends on the business’s resources, risk appetite and strategic goals.

Key Fact

Internal growth uses the business’s own resources — launching new products, entering new markets or investing in research and development. External growth is faster but involves acquiring or merging with another business.

Internal (Organic) Growth

Internal growth comes from within the business itself. A company might invest in research and development (R&D) to launch innovative products that attract new customers. Alternatively, it can enter new markets — for example, a UK clothing brand opening an online store to sell internationally, or changing its pricing and promotion to attract a different customer segment. Technology has made internal expansion faster: e-commerce platforms let a small business sell to customers worldwide without the cost of physical stores.

Internal growth is generally lower risk because it builds on what the business already knows. It avoids the problems of integrating a different company’s culture, systems and staff. However, it is usually slower than external growth and relies on generating enough cash or profit to fund expansion.

External (Inorganic) Growth

External growth involves combining with or taking over another business. A merger is when two businesses voluntarily agree to join together. A takeover is when one business purchases a controlling interest in another — this can be agreed or hostile. External growth is quicker than organic growth and can give a business immediate access to new markets, brands, technology or skilled staff. For example, a supermarket chain acquiring a smaller rival instantly gains its store network, customer base and supplier contracts.

External growth can be very attractive because it is fast and removes a competitor at the same time. Mergers and takeovers can create economies of scale — the combined business can buy supplies in larger quantities and reduce per-unit costs. However, integrating two different companies is complex and expensive. Staff may be made redundant, cultures may clash and customers can become confused if brand identities merge poorly. Some takeovers have destroyed shareholder value when the purchase price was too high or the two businesses were a poor strategic fit.

Public Limited Companies (plc)

As a business grows, it may need more capital than its owners or bank can provide. One option is to convert to a public limited company (plc). A plc floats its shares on the stock market through a process called stock market flotation. Members of the public, investment funds and other businesses can then buy shares. This raises large amounts of capital that can fund rapid expansion, research or acquisitions. Well-known UK plcs include Tesco, Marks & Spencer and Rolls-Royce.

Becoming a plc brings significant benefits but also serious obligations. Shareholders expect dividends and rising share prices. The company must publish detailed financial accounts, making its performance visible to competitors. Directors can face pressure from institutional investors to deliver short-term profits, which may conflict with long-term growth strategies.

Key Fact

Growing businesses can use internal finance (retained profit and selling assets) or external finance (loan capital and share capital). Only public limited companies can raise share capital via stock market flotation.

Sources of Finance for Growth

A growing business has four main sources of finance. Retained profit is the most flexible internal source — no interest to pay and no loss of ownership. A business can also raise cash by selling assets it no longer needs, such as unused machinery or a surplus property. These internal sources avoid debt but may be limited in size.

External sources include loan capital, which provides a lump sum but requires regular repayments and interest charges. The second external source is share capital. For a private limited company (Ltd), new shares can only be sold to people the owners choose. A plc can sell shares to the general public on the stock exchange, giving access to far larger sums. The trade-off is that each new shareholder owns a slice of the business and has voting rights at annual meetings.

Students often confuse “internal growth” with “internal finance” — these are separate ideas. Internal growth means expanding by using the business’s own capabilities (new products, new markets). Internal finance means funding expansion using money already inside the business (retained profit or asset sales). A business can pursue internal growth using external finance (e.g. taking a bank loan to fund a new product launch), or external growth using internal finance (e.g. using retained profit to fund a takeover). Keep the two concepts clearly separated in your answers.
exam_tip_html: On a 6-mark Explain question about growth methods, only your best two points are credited — write two well-developed points, each with a statement of fact and two logical expansion sentences. Do not rush on to a third point. For 9-mark Analyse in Context questions, the examiner wants to see specific details from the case-study scenario (the product, location, financial figures, customer base) woven into your analysis — naming the business alone does not earn application marks. For 12-mark Justify questions, you do not need to discuss both options in equal depth: a fully developed argument for one recommendation, with a contextualised reason for rejecting the alternative, can reach the top tier.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Internal (organic) growth comes from within — new products, new markets, or technology — and is lower risk but slower than external growth.
  • External (inorganic) growth via mergers or takeovers is faster but carries integration risks; only a plc can raise finance through stock market flotation.
  • Growing businesses can use four sources of finance: retained profit and selling assets (internal), or loan capital and share capital (external).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of internal (organic) growth?
A) Acquiring a rival company through a takeover
B) Merging with a supplier to reduce costs
C) Launching a new product range funded by retained profit
D) Floating shares on the stock exchange for the first time
practice_questions.marks: C) Launching a new product range funded by retained profit [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two internal sources of finance available to a growing business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each correct source (up to 2 marks):
• Retained profit
• Selling assets
[2 marks maximum]

practice_questions.text: Outline one advantage and one disadvantage of a business choosing external (inorganic) growth through a takeover.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantage (1 mark for the point + 1 mark for development):
• A takeover gives rapid access to new markets, customers or technology without having to build them from scratch, meaning the business can grow much faster than through organic methods.

Disadvantage (1 mark for the point, 0 development marks needed for the third mark as only 3 total):
• Integrating the acquired business can be costly and disruptive — staff redundancies, cultural clashes and system changes can reduce productivity and increase costs in the short term.

[3 marks: 1 for advantage point, 1 for development of advantage, 1 for a clear disadvantage point]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a business might choose to become a public limited company (plc) rather than remain a private limited company (Ltd).
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for the two best-developed points only:

Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed points, each with a clear statement and two logical expansion sentences that connect cause to effect for a plc specifically.

Secure (3-4 marks): Two points made, at least one with clear development showing why becoming a plc helps the business achieve its aims.

Developing (1-2 marks): One or two simple points with limited development, such as 'a plc can sell shares to the public'.

Emergent (0 marks): No relevant business knowledge demonstrated.

Content that could be credited:
• Becoming a plc enables the business to raise large amounts of capital through stock market flotation — this provides funds for major investment, acquisitions or expansion into new markets that would be impossible to finance from retained profit or bank loans alone.
• As a plc, the owners benefit from limited liability — shareholders can only lose the amount they invested, making it easier to attract investors who might otherwise be put off by personal financial risk.
• A plc can use its publicly traded shares as currency for acquisitions, offering its own shares rather than cash to buy other businesses, reducing the need for large cash reserves.

practice_questions.text:
Hartwell Engineering Ltd is a precision engineering firm based in the West Midlands with 85 employees and annual revenue of £4.2 million. The owner, Priya Hartwell, has been approached by a German competitor that wants to merge. Priya is also considering pursuing organic growth by investing in new CNC machinery to expand the product range.

Analyse the benefits and drawbacks of Hartwell Engineering Ltd choosing to merge with the German competitor rather than investing in new machinery.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): Sustained analysis using specific details from the scenario (Hartwell's 85 staff, £4.2m revenue, precision engineering specialism, West Midlands location) to evaluate the merger versus organic investment. Both benefits and drawbacks are analysed with clear chains of reasoning linked to Hartwell's specific context.

Secure (5-7 marks): Clear analysis of at least two points, with relevant use of context but possibly missing some scenario specifics. Both sides considered but may not be fully balanced.

Developing (3-4 marks): Some relevant points about mergers or organic growth, but analysis is generic and does not use Hartwell's specific details. Limited exploration of consequences.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic identification of a benefit or drawback with no development or context.

Content that could be credited:
• Merging with the German competitor would give Hartwell immediate access to European markets and a broader customer base, potentially growing revenue far beyond what £4.2m organic growth could achieve — but the culture and language differences could create significant integration challenges for an 85-person firm without a dedicated HR or integration team.
• The merger could bring access to the German company's technology or processes, removing the need to invest in new CNC machinery separately — however, if the German firm's equipment is incompatible, costs could escalate.
• Organic investment preserves Priya's sole control over the direction of the business, whereas a merger would dilute ownership and introduce new decision-makers who may not share her vision for the West Midlands operation.

practice_questions.text:
Cobblestone Candles is a handmade candle brand founded three years ago by Sofia Reyes in Manchester. It currently operates as a sole trader and sells through farmers markets and a small website. Revenue has grown to £180,000 per year. Sofia is considering two options:

Option A: Convert to a private limited company (Ltd) and reinvest profits to launch a national online store.
Option B: Seek a merger with a larger home-fragrance brand to gain immediate national distribution.

Justify which option Sofia should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): A fully developed recommendation for one option, supported by specific analysis linked to the scenario details (£180,000 revenue, sole trader status, Manchester location, handmade product, online + farmers market channels). Clear evaluative conclusion that acknowledges the rejected option's appeal but explains why the chosen option better suits Cobblestone Candles' context.

Secure (7-9 marks): A clear recommendation with developed analysis of relevant advantages and at least one reason for rejecting the alternative. Uses some scenario context.

Developing (4-6 marks): A preference is stated and some relevant points are made, but the argument is largely generic and could apply to any business rather than Cobblestone Candles specifically.

Emerging (1-3 marks): A basic recommendation with little or no development or context.

Content that could be credited in favour of Option A (Ltd + organic growth):
• Converting to a Ltd protects Sofia's personal assets through limited liability, making further investment less personally risky as the business scales.
• Retaining full ownership means Sofia controls how the brand develops — crucial for a handmade, artisan brand where the founder's identity is closely linked to customer loyalty.
• At £180,000 revenue, the business may not yet need the scale a merger brings — organic growth lets Sofia test national demand through e-commerce with lower overhead.

Content that could be credited in favour of Option B (merger):
• A merger with a larger distributor gives immediate national shelf space, far outpacing what organic digital growth could achieve in the short term.
• The larger partner may bring warehousing, logistics and marketing resources that Sofia cannot afford alone.

Expected recommendation (Option A is stronger for this context): Sofia's brand identity as a handmade, founder-led product risks being diluted in a merger; converting to Ltd and investing in organic e-commerce growth preserves that identity while managing personal financial risk.

knowledge_checks.q: What is a merger in business?
options: When one business forces another to sell its shares
When two businesses voluntarily agree to combine into one
When a business sells assets to raise finance
When a business launches a new product line

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an EXTERNAL source of finance?
options: Retaining profit from the previous year
Borrowing money as a bank loan

knowledge_checks.q: Internal growth is also known as _____ growth.
A public limited company can raise share capital through a process called stock market _____.
Match each term to its correct definition:
right: Money borrowed from a bank and repaid with interest
Profit reinvested in the business after tax and dividends
When a company first offers shares to the general public

flashcard_questions.a: Growth achieved from within the business by launching new products, entering new markets or using technology.
Growth achieved by merging with or taking over another business.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a merger and a takeover?
flashcard_questions.a: A merger is a voluntary combination of two firms; a takeover is when one buys a controlling stake in another.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a public limited company (plc)?
flashcard_questions.a: A business whose shares are listed on a stock exchange and can be bought by the general public.
When a company first offers its shares to the public by listing on a stock exchange.

flashcard_questions.q: Retained profit = revenue minus costs minus tax minus ____.
What is retained profit as a source of finance?
flashcard_questions.a: Profit kept inside the business after tax and dividends, reinvested to fund growth.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one advantage of using retained profit over a bank loan for growth.
flashcard_questions.a: No interest payments and no loss of ownership or control.
Money borrowed from a bank or lender, repaid with interest over an agreed period.
Money raised by selling part-ownership of the business to investors in exchange for shares.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might a plc face pressure to make short-term profits?
flashcard_questions.a: Shareholders expect dividends and a rising share price, which can override long-term growth plans.

flashcard_questions.q: Which type of business can raise capital through stock market flotation — Ltd or plc?
Give one risk of external growth through a takeover.
flashcard_questions.a: Cultural clashes and integration costs can reduce productivity and erode the value of the acquisition.

glossary_terms.definition: Growth achieved from within the business by increasing sales, launching new products or entering new markets — also called organic growth.
Growth achieved by joining with or acquiring another business through a merger or takeover — also called inorganic growth.
The process of creating and refining new products or processes, typically funded by the business to give it a competitive edge.
When two businesses agree to combine and form a single new company.
When one business buys a controlling stake in another, sometimes against the wishes of the target company's board.
A business that has issued shares to the public on a stock exchange and whose shareholders have limited liability.
When a company first offers its shares to the public by listing on a stock exchange, often called an Initial Public Offering (IPO).
Profit kept within the business after tax and dividends have been paid, reinvested to fund growth or operations.
Money borrowed from a bank or other lender that must be repaid with interest over an agreed period.
Money raised by selling shares in the business, giving shareholders part-ownership in return for their investment.
